The goal of the Capital Planning Committee is to provide a means of planning for necessary expenditures for maintenance, equipment, and/ or improvements of the capital assets and infrastructure of the Town of Lunenburg.
The Capital Planning Committee shall research, study and advise the Selectmen and Finance Committee of the requests for short and long-range capital purchases for the Town. The Committee shall be charged with facilitating the coordination between community objectives, capital needs, and fiscal capacity. The Committee will help the Town to understand the tax impact of the capital expenditures and consider the relative need, timing, and cost of each capital expenditure. The Committee shall consider all written requests and make recommendations. The Committee shall provide a written report to assist the Selectmen and Finance Committee in keeping the community informed about the Town's future anticipated needs and projects that will be voted on at the Annual Town Meeting.
The Capital Planning Committee receives its authorization from Article 27 of the Town's Bylaws which states, "There shall be a Capital Planning Committee. That Committee shall consist of five members to be appointed as follows: One member each designated by the Financial Committee, the Select Board, the School Committee, and the Planning Board, and a fifth member chosen at large by the Town Moderator. Each member shall be appointed for a term of three years, said terms staggered so that nearly an equal number of members shall be appointed each year. The Capital Planning Committee shall establish and update a comprehensive capital plan.
The committee shall at least annually provide its materials to the Chief Administrative and Financial Officer so that the Chief Administrative and Financial Officer will meet the obligations of the Office set forth in Section 6-6 (sic) of the Lunenburg Town Charter. The Capital Planning Committee shall be responsible for providing a complete inventory of town property, real and personal, including school property, in conjunction with the Chief Administrative and Financial Officer. page.overview:
The Cemetery Commission is an elected three-member Commission with terms of three years each. The board of cemetery commissioners have the responsibility to make regulations governing the care, superintendence, and management of all public burial grounds in Lunenburg and to lay out existing public burial grounds and may lot out in lots or other suitable subdivision with proper paths, lanes, and ways appropriate for burial use any other land acquired by the town for burial purposes. The day-to-day care and maintenance of the cemeteries shall be under the supervision of the Town Manager, which has been delegated to the DPW Director as the Cemetery is a division under the Department of Public Works.
Lunenburg has two major cemeteries:
North Cemetery is located on Holman Street at the corner of Highland Street
South Cemetery is located on Page Street off Lancaster Avenue

page.overview:
At least once every ten years a special committee consisting of nine members shall be established for the purpose of reviewing the Town Charter and making a report, with recommendations, to the Town Meeting concerning proposed amendments which said committee may determine to be necessary or desirable. The committee shall consist of nine members who shall be chosen as follows: the Select Board, the Finance Committee and the School Committee shall each designate two persons, the Planning Board shall designate one person and two persons shall be appointed by the Town Moderator.
Persons appointed by the agencies may, but need not be members of the agency by which they are designated. The committee shall organize forthwith following the final adjournment of the Annual Town Meeting.
Members and Contact Information are to be determined.

page.overview:
The Lunenburg Cultural Council is responsible for disbursing funds received from the Massachusetts Cultural Council for local cultural and artistic activities.
The mission of the Lunenburg Cultural Council is to nurture and promote a diverse range of artistic and cultural programs for the benefit of Lunenburg and surrounding communities.
We accomplish this through the annual allocation of state grants for local projects and by producing cultural events using locally-raised funds.
The Council reviews proposals and grants funds to local applicants for a variety of projects that benefit Lunenburg citizens. Local Cultural Councils support community-based projects in the arts, sciences, and humanities every year. The state legislature provides an annual appropriation to the Massachusetts Cultural Council, a state agency, which then allocates funds to each community.
The Lunenburg Cultural Council recognizes that the arts, humanities, and interpretive sciences form an important part of Lunenburg's history, identity, and vision. We are committed to nurturing our artistic community through supporting events that are accessible, collaborative, and fun for Lunenburg residents and visitors of all ages.

page.overview:
Section 1: General
The Lunenburg Economic Development Committee is being formed by the Planning Board in order to better assist, counsel, and advise the residents of Lunenburg, the Planning Board, other Town Boards and Departments, and Lunenburg businesses on ways to promote the local economy.
Section 2: Functions
Mission: The Lunenburg Economic Development Committee is committed to promoting business development that will enhance the character, culture, and commerce in Lunenburg. The Committee shall investigate current economic conditions to provide advice to Town Departments on economic development policy; meet and work with current Lunenburg businesses and prospective businesses; coordinate its activities with the appropriate Town Boards and Commissions; and work cooperatively with businesses and state agencies to retain, develop and promote businesses in Lunenburg.
Section 3: Membership & Meetings
The Committee shall be composed of five regular members serving three-year terms appointed by the Planning Board as follows: One member recommended by the Agricultural Commission that owns a business in Lunenburg and shall initially be appointed for a three-year term; One member recommended by the Open Space Committee and shall initially be appointed for a three-year term; One member recommended by the Conservation Commission and shall initially be appointed for a two-year term; Two members that are residents of Lunenburg, one shall initially be appointed for a two-year term and one shall initially be appointed for a one year term. In addition to the regular members, there will be four ex-officio members as follows: One member of the Select Board chosen annually by the Select Board; One member of the Planning Board chosen annually by the Planning Board; The Director of Planning and Economic Development; and A Lunenburg Business Owner.
After the initial term, all members shall serve a three-year term.
Voting Power: All duly appointed members shall have full voting power; ex-officio members shall not have the power to vote.
Resignation: Members of the Committee shall notify the Chairman of the Committee and the Planning Board of their resignation.
Vacancies: Any vacancies shall be filled in the same manner as the original appointment.
The election of officers including at least a Chairman, Vice-Chairman, and Clerk and shall be elected annually by a majority vote of the Committee.
A quorum shall consist of three members.
The Committee shall keep a recording of minutes and votes of all meetings as prescribed by the Open Meeting Law. This charge may be amended at any time.
New way to complete your Business Identity Certificate:
For people planning on opening a new business in Lunenburg, the Town Clerk’s NEW Business Identity Certificate (BIC) is now available to be completed as part of Building Department’s Form of Intent found here: Business Identity Certificate (BIC) You will still need to print out the BIC and hand-deliver to the Town Clerk’s office, but now the form can be completed and generated online.
New Business Ribbon Cutting Ceremony:
On Thursday August 6, the Town of Lunenburg's Economic Development Committee proudly hosted its first ribbon cutting ceremony, celebrating the continued growth of Diligent Digital Marketing Corp. as the company expands into a larger office in Lunenburg. The event welcomed the business to its new space at 1 Main Street and marked the beginning of a new tradition recognizing business investment and success in our community.
Founded by Chris Kostecki, Diligent Digital Marketing Corp. has grown from a sole proprietorship into a full-service digital marketing consulting firm.
Chris was joined by members of his family, Economic Development Committee Members Joeci Gilchrest and Cathy Clark, State Representative Mike Kushmerek, State Representative Margaret Scarsdale, Beth Walsh, Constituent Services Director for State Senator John Cronin, Roy Nascimento, President & CEO of the North Central Massachusetts Chamber of Commerce, Chamber Staff and Members, Select Board members Renee Emkey, Brian Lehtinen, and Glenn McLeod, and Town Manager Jennifer Warren-Dyment.
Congratulations to Chris and the entire Diligent team on this exciting milestone. We wish you continued success and are proud that your business continues to grow right here in Lunenburg.

Section 1: General
The Lunenburg Green Communities Committee will work with the Massachusetts Department of Energy Resources to learn of grant opportunities for energy conservation and renewable energy generation and will apply for appropriate grants. The Committee will ensure the Town retains its status as a designated Green Community.
Section 2: Functions
Mission: The Lunenburg Green Communities Committee will focus on improving and promoting energy efficiency in town and school facilities, infrastructure, and vehicles. The Committee will help raise awareness, educate, advise, and motivate the Town of Lunenburg residents and businesses to reduce waste, reduce energy use, conserve resources, reduce emissions/carbon footprint, and embrace clean and renewable energy options.
Responsibilities
Identify and develop grant submissions for Green Communities Competitive Grant annually that corresponds with the mission of this committee and is consistent with the Town's goals;
Develop action steps to ensure Lunenburg remains designated as a Department of Energy Resources Green Community;
Facilitate town participation in DOER programs, grants, and incentives;
Serve as an information resource for town residents and business owners on the benefits of energy and resource conservation;
Increase constituents' awareness of and promote resource conservation methods, energy efficiency programs, utility rebates, and state/federal programs to promote energy efficiency, waste reduction, recycling, and overall enhancements to long-term sustainability and resilience in response to environmental, resource, and energy challenges;
Report at least once annually on its activities to the Select Board.
Section 3: Membership & Meetings
The Committee shall be composed of 5 regular members serving three-year terms appointed by the Select Board and two associate members. Two members shall initially be appointed to a three-year term, two members shall initially be appointed to a two-year term, and one member shall initially be appointed to a one-year term. After the initial term, all regular members shall serve a three-year term. The associate members shall be appointed to a three-year term.
In addition to the regular members, the Committee shall consult with the Town Manager, the town departments that oversee the facilities and energy accounts, the School Superintendent, and the School Facilities Director that oversees the school facilities and school energy accounts in order to ascertain future energy projects, areas where energy savings are needed, and replacement schedule for vehicles.
Voting Power: All duly appointed regular members shall have full voting power.
Resignation: Members of the Committee shall notify the Chairman of the Committee, the Town Manager, and the Select Board of their resignation.
Vacancies: Any vacancies shall be filled in the same manner as the original appointment.
Representations: Members shall get the approval of the Committee prior to making statements, presentations, or joining activities on behalf of the Committee.
The election of officers including at least a Chairman, Vice-Chairman, and Clerk and shall be elected annually by a majority vote of the Committee.
A quorum shall consist of three members.
The recording of minutes and votes of all meetings shall be conducted as prescribed by the Open Meeting Law. Copies of the minutes shall be submitted to the Town Clerk as prescribed in the Town Bylaw and according to Open Meeting Law.
The Committee shall comply with all state laws and local bylaws.
This charge was adopted by the Select Board at their June 1, 2021 meeting and may be amended at any future meeting.

The Historical Commission shall act for the preservation, protection, and development of the historical or archeological assets of the Town. The commission shall conduct research for places of historic or archeological value, shall seek to coordinate the activities of unofficial bodies organized for similar purposes, and may advertise, prepare, print, and distribute materials that it deems necessary for its work. It shall make recommendations to the Select Board that any place be certified as a historical landmark. The commission may hold hearings and may enter into contracts with individuals, organizations, and institutions for services furthering their objectives.
The commission may acquire in the name of the Town by gift, purchase, grant, bequest, devise, lease, or otherwise, the fee or lesser interest in real or personal property of significant historical value and may manage the same. The commission shall file an annual report which shall be included in the Annual Town Report.
The Historical Commission shall be composed of five (5) members appointed by the Select Board for terms of three years each with said terms staggered so that as nearly an equal number of members shall be appointed each year.

Lunenburg Public Library welcomes all and serves residents of the Lunenburg area as a hub for the community, enriching our lives through its collections, programs, services, facility, and people.
Please visit the Lunenburg Public Library Website for library resources, latest news, and events.
Powers and Duties - The Board of Trustees shall act as an agent of the public trust governing the library. The library shall create the general operating and administrative policies relating to budget, personnel, and contracts as specified by state law and local ordinances. All funds raised or appropriated by the town for the support and maintenance of the library shall be expended under the direction of the board. All funds that the town may receive by gift, bequest, or otherwise for library purposes shall be administered under the direction of the board in accordance with the terms of such gift, bequest, or otherwise. The board shall hire and manage the library director. The responsibilities and governance of the board shall cover the following specific areas: (i) legal; (ii) policy making; (iii) financial governance; and (iv) strategic planning. The board shall, in all matters of general municipal policy and procedure, be subject to policy directives designed to achieve uniformity and better administrative control as may from time to time be established by the town manager. The library director shall exercise professional judgment under the direction and review of the board to implement the strategic objectives and policies set by the board. The library director shall be responsible for the day-to-day administration of the library, including management of personnel, collection development, budget, physical plant, and programmatic functions, subject to policy directives established by the board. The library director shall work in conjunction with the board on strategic planning and library policies.
The Library Director shall prepare an annual budget for approval by the board. The library director shall hire library employees, fix their salaries, define their duties, make rules concerning their tenure of office and discharge them in accordance with and within the limits established by the town personnel by-laws, policies, procedures, and practices and any applicable collective bargaining agreement, in accordance with municipal policies. The board shall make all reasonable rules and regulations for the operation and management of the library system and for the conduct of its own business and affairs as may be deemed necessary. The board shall have all of the other powers and duties that are given to library trustees by general law, this charter, by-law, or other vote of the town meeting.
Composition, Term of Office - There shall be a board of trustees of the public library consisting of 7 members, elected for terms of 3 years each, so arranged that the terms of as nearly an equal number of members as is possible shall expire each year.

page.overview:
The year 2028 will mark the 300th Anniversary of the incorporation of the Town of Lunenburg. In order to recognize and celebrate Lunenburg's Tricentennial, the residents of Lunenburg, by Town Meeting vote of May 7, 2022, authorized and established a steering committee, subsequently designated the "Lunenburg 300th Anniversary Committee," and hereinafter referred to as "the Committee."
The Committee shall be comprised of no greater than 11 members, each of whom shall be appointed by the Select Board for a term to begin on the date of appointment and terminate when, as determined by a vote of the Select Board, the Committee has discharged all of its defined functions and is dissolved. As a body, the Committee shall:
Develop a celebratory plan including a timeline, proposed events, publicity plan, volunteer roster, funding requirements, and funding sources.
Coordinate with other entities and officials within the Town government, including the police chief, fire chief, DPW director, historical commission, and superintendent of schools, in order to facilitate safety and maximize resident participation.
Solicit, evaluate, and generate recommendations as to how the Town should manage the commemoration of its tricentennial, and the celebration of its rich history.
Oversee subcommittees established for specified purposes, and supervise and assist these subcommittees in their functions.
Recruit, organize, task, and oversee volunteers from among the townspeople in furtherance of the overall celebration and the execution of specific functions of the Committee and/or its subcommittees.
Plan, coordinate, manage, sponsored, and implement commemorative events including, but not limited to, recreational and educational activities and social/cultural gatherings intended to enhance the townspeople's awareness and appreciation for the history of the Town and the contributions that its residents have made locally and nationally to various fields of human endeavor including, for example, architecture, arts, civil rights, government, engineering, environmental protection, industry, invention, law, literature, medicine, the military, politics, public policy, public safety, and science.
Encourage through effective communication and outreach maximum inclusion, attendance, and participation by the townspeople in events and celebrations.
Partner with local businesses and community organizations to develop events that appeal to all ages and encourage maximum participation by town residents.

page.overview:
The Lunenburg Municipal Building Design Committee (formerly the TC Passios Building Design Committee) will continue to work with any contracted architectural and engineering firms, as they become available, to review space needs for town offices, school uses and community space at the building and/or land known as the TC Passios.
Additionally, the committee will work to prioritize and/or rank the existing space usage requests and explore a variety of design permutations at different estimated budget tiers that would meet the needs of the Town according to those priorities. The committee may analyze, discuss and investigate other Town-owned buildings and properties in their recommendations as they deem necessary to fulfill this charge.
This Committee will prepare viable, cost-effective solutions for the Select Board that conform to all the Town's existing financial and fiscal policies and take into consideration any/all large-scale capital expenditures projected for the next 10 years. This charge was amended by the Select Board at their January 4, 2022 meeting and may be amended at any future meeting. At the July 15, 2025 meeting of the Select Board, it was voted to add a member from the Architectural Preservation District Commission to the composition of the LMBDC and reduced the quorum to four.

page.overview:
The Planning Board has designated updating the Master Plan as a priority. The new Master Plan will be used as a guide for the Town of Lunenburg in the areas of land use, economic development, housing, transportation, community services, and capital/facilities planning among others. The development of the Master Plan is a primary statutory function of the Planning Board.
Over two decades old, the 2002 Lunenburg Master Plan sought to provide recommendations and an implementation plan for addressing the impacts of residential growth including identifying strategies for land use, economic development, natural and cultural resources, housing, transportation, and community services and facilities. In the twenty-one years since, Lunenburg has experienced significant changes in land use and population growth. The updated Master Plan will reflect, among other things, changes to the Zoning Code, current projects, new environmental and other regulatory constraints, and plan for appropriate land uses to support the long and short‐term needs of the community, with a look to retaining the rural nature, agricultural base, and natural character that exist. The concepts of community sustainability and resiliency will be considered throughout the Master Plan and permeate all topic areas.
The Plan is intended to be a consensus vision of the residents of Lunenburg and all efforts will be made to include as many voices as feasible in its development. Items identified for consideration in the Master Plan update include, but are not limited to the following:
Identifying areas for Inclusionary Zoning and other Affordable Housing measures
Examining places for public use spaces and amenities
Identifying sustainable environmental measures
Analyzing the impact of new residential development on the public schools and other Town services
Evaluating infrastructure needs for the area
Strategizing economic development measures to entice businesses to town, while maintaining its rural feel
Expanding economic opportunities for existing and new agricultural uses
Charge
The Master Plan Steering Committee advises on the development of the Master Plan document. The Committee also fosters openness and inclusion in the master planning process through dialogue and communication with the consulting team of OverUnder, RKG, Innes Associates, and various stakeholders in the Lunenburg Community.
Vision
The Master Plan will develop a physical and digital document for the Town of Lunenburg that optimally reflects and supports the Community’s priorities and goals.
Membership
The Master Plan Steering Committee is comprised of designated Lunenburg Board and Committee members, and several at‐large community members. The Committee is guided and led by the
Planning Board, OverUnder/RKG/Innes Associates, the Master Plan Consultants, and the Land Use Department. Membership will be in existence for approximately 18 to 24 months to direct the preparation of the Master Plan.
The Master Plan Steering Committee shall be convened and charged by the Planning Board. Members will be appointed for the term of the update process.
The Committee shall consist of 15 voting members, as follows:
One members of the Planning Board, appointed by the Planning Board
One members of the Board of Selectmen, appointed by the Board of Selectmen
One member of the Conservation Commission, appointed by the Conservation Commission
One member of the Council on Aging, appointed by the Council on Aging.
One member of the Parks and Recreation Commission, appointed by the Parks and Recreation Commission
One member of the Lunenburg School Committee, appointed by the Lunenburg School Committee
One member of the Lunenburg Library Trustees appointed by the Lunenburg Library Trustees
One member of the Zoning Board of Appeals, appointed by the Zoning Board of Appeals
One member of the Finance Committee, appointed by the Finance Committee
Six members at large, appointed by the Planning Board
The Master Plan Steering Committee shall appoint a Chair and Vice Chair to guide its efforts and a Clerk to maintain the record of the Committee. The Master Plan Steering Committee shall appoint subcommittees as it deems necessary to the fulfillment of its duties.
Final approval of the Master Plan will be subject to the Planning Board upon completion of the document by the consulting team and Master Plan Steering Committee.

page.overview:
The Open Space Committee is a seven-member board whose bylaws can be found at the Code of Lunenburg, Chapter 12, Article IX.
The Committee’s primary duties are:
Produce and update Lunenburg’s Open Space Plan and Recreation Plan
Assist and advise other Town boards/committees regarding the use/acquisition of open space areas for the community
Review Chapter 61 conversions and make recommendations to the Select Board
Maintain an inventory of open space in Lunenburg
Lunenburg’s current Open Space and Recreation Plan update covers a ten-year window, July 1, 2019 to June 30, 2029, as prescribed by the Massachusetts Executive Office of Energy and Environmental Affairs. The Plan provides both a planning and action framework to address current and future needs of conservation and recreation land, agricultural land, corridors and parks, and greenways. Meeting agendas and minutes are posted and available on the Town's website to update the public.

page.overview:
Please visit the Lunenburg Recreation Website for events, activities, and general information.
The Park Commissioners may layout and improve public parks, make rules for their use and government, and appoint all necessary engineers, surveyors, clerks, and other officers, including a police force to act in such parks. The Park Commissioners may define the powers and duties of that police force, fix the compensation of its members and do all acts necessary for the proper execution of its powers and duties. Subject to appropriation, the Park Commissioners may conduct park programs and recreation activities at locations other than the public parks. The day-to-day care and maintenance of the public parks shall be under the supervision of the Town Manager.
The Park Commission consists of five members elected for terms of three years each so arranged that the term of office of one member shall expire each year.

watch_next: Wallace Park lighting vote expected at the next meeting, September 30
Field usage fee schedule consensus targeted for October or November, with a full commission present to vote

what_happened.line: The Parks Commission approved town beach access for a November 28 Polar Plunge fundraiser.
The commission held off voting on replacing old mercury lights at Wallace Park's basketball courts, pending a quote timeline, disposal cost, and possible state grant funding.
Before committing to that lighting upgrade, the commission wants a policy on hours of use and neighbor notification.
A draft memorandum of understanding on recreation department use of library rooms remains unsigned; a revised draft is due for review next month.
The commission will keep reviewing field and court usage fees this fall, aiming for consensus by October or November.

why_it_matters: A Wallace Park lighting upgrade would likely be paid from the parks revolving account or a Green Communities Act grant rather than the tax levy, but no funding source or cost is settled yet.
Field and court usage fees, described as unchanged for years, could rise for youth sports leagues and residents who rent town fields and courts.
The library-recreation MOU will set the terms under which town recreation programs can keep using library meeting rooms going forward.

ours.headline: Parks Commission OK'd beach access for a fundraiser and is weighing a $2,200 Wallace Park lighting upgrade

watch_next: Town accountant's input on the Town Beach salary/revenue question, expected before a season-extension decision
Next scheduled meeting, moved to September 30th

what_happened.line: Parks Commission tabled extending Town Beach's season, saying the May fee increase brought in less than the department expected.
The beach's town-appropriated salary line was already mostly spent partway into the season, meaning any extension would draw from the beach revolving account instead.
An unlocked irrigation controller at Marshall Park was changed by a user group and ran far longer than intended, producing an unusually high water bill.
The commission declined to sign a draft space-use agreement with the library, opting to wait for the library trustees' specific concerns.
The commission voted to appoint a commissioner to the town's Open Space Committee and approved two sets of minutes.

why_it_matters: A Town Beach season extension depends on money not yet in hand: whether fee revenue and day-pass sales catch up, and whether the town accountant confirms the salary line can absorb it.
The Marshall Park water overrun and a request to match each water bill to its field point toward how field/facility costs get tracked and billed going forward, not a settled dollar figure yet.
Any library or school-district space-sharing arrangement is still under discussion, so no agreement currently binds either side.

ours.headline: Commission tabled extending Town Beach hours after fee revenue fell short of what the May increase was expected to bring in

watch_next: Skatepark right-of-entry/escrow agreement returns for a commission vote once both attorneys and the funder have weighed in
May 27th minutes come back for approval, and the vacant Open Space Committee seat, at the July 22 meeting

what_happened.line: The skatepark right-of-entry and escrow agreement was not put to a vote; it still needs review by the group's attorney and town counsel before it returns to the board.
The commission voted to endorse a new mission statement for the Recreation Department.
The board set a cap on spending for a ceremony renaming the town beach house for Genevieve Nass, keeping costs to what it called a minimum.
Approval of last month's minutes was tabled after a member could not open the town's SharePoint folder where they were posted.
The commission confirmed its next two meeting dates.

why_it_matters: The skatepark project, years and a large public fundraising effort in, still has no signed agreement with the town, so construction cannot move ahead until both attorneys clear the terms.
The new mission statement sets the stated direction for Recreation Department programming that residents' camps, sports and beach activities run under.
The beach house dedication is a small, capped town expense, and the tabled minutes reflect an access problem rather than a dispute over their content.

ours.headline: Skatepark's new town right-of-entry/escrow deal awaits attorney review; no vote taken yet

watch_next: Next Parks Commission meeting, June 24, 2026
Revised mission statement draft and periodic financial reports on the revolving-account trial

what_happened.line: The Parks Commission voted to fund the part-time recreation director's FY27 salary entirely from the department's revolving account, as a one-year trial toward a self-sustaining position.
The commission elected Chris Sullivan as chair and Dan Burns as vice chair as longtime chair Karen Bernard prepares to step down.
The commission approved a request from LHS baseball boosters to replace the memorial scoreboard at Marshall Park's 90-foot diamond.
The commission declined to create a discounted seasonal field rate for a short-season youth baseball league, keeping the standard fee with hardship scholarships available instead.
The skate park project remains stalled, still awaiting review by town counsel.

why_it_matters: Paying the recreation director's salary out of program revenue rather than the tax-supported budget is a funding-mechanism shift for the position, with a strategic plan and periodic financial reporting required to track whether it works.
The scoreboard vote and field-fee decision affect who uses Marshall Park and on what terms, including families weighing a hardship scholarship application over a standard rental fee.
The change in commission leadership and a still-unresolved skate park review affect who sets Parks policy going forward and when that project can move.

ours.headline: Parks Commission votes to fund the part-time recreation director's FY27 salary from its revolving account as a one-year trial

watch_next: A future Commission vote on the skate park right-of-entry agreement, once the town attorney returns it with the bond-funding document incorporated
The April 28 budget/override meet-and-greet

what_happened.line: The Commission voted to waive Marshall Park T-ball user fees for the season if youth baseball does the field maintenance, and banned dogs from that field for the season.
The board also agreed the new Recreation Director can spend from her programming budget line and approve new field-rental vendors on file insurance alone, without a commission vote each time.
The skate park's right-of-entry agreement remains with the town attorney, who must incorporate the project's bond-funding document before it comes back for a commission vote.
A vendor-fair dump-tank rental, to be funded from the parks revolving account, was discussed and moved, but the vote's outcome was not audible in the recording.

why_it_matters: Delegating budget and vendor-approval authority to the Recreation Director means some routine parks and recreation decisions will no longer come before the Commission as a public vote.
Marshall Park users should expect a no-dogs rule at the T-ball field for the rest of the season.
The skate park project's next step is a legal document, not a commission decision, so its timeline depends on the town attorney's office.

ours.headline: Commission waived T-ball field fees, went no-dogs there for the season; skate park still awaits town attorney

watch_next: Exact dunk-tank rental pricing for one-day versus two-day/rain-date options, due before the next meeting
The FY27 override vote and budget decision at town meeting

what_happened.line: Under the town's proposed FY27 balanced budget, the recreation director position would be eliminated and beach funding cut, closing the town beach next summer.
Two override tiers were outlined: one restores a part-time director and some programming, the other funds a full-time director; both keep the beach open.
The board voted to partner with the Lunenburg Business Association to run the 2026 vendor fair, with no town staff support provided.
The board voted to authorize renting a dunk tank for the fair before the next meeting if needed.
Facility staff will price prepping the Marshall T-ball field for possible use, with a dog-ban decision to follow if it is opened up.

why_it_matters: The FY27 balanced-budget scenario would end the town beach and the recreation director job, a service and a position that would return only if voters approve an override.
Residents will be asked to choose among a no-override, part-time-director, or full-time-director budget path that decides what recreation programming exists next year.
The vendor-fair partnership hands event logistics to the business association rather than town staff, which limits what municipal resources back the event.

ours.headline: Board warns FY27's balanced-budget scenario would eliminate the recreation director and close the town beach

watch_next: Next Parks Commission meeting, March 25, 2026
Written response to Lunenburg Youth Baseball on the proposed vendor-fair partnership, once a recreation director is hired

what_happened.line: The Parks Commission voted to raise 2026 Town Beach season and day pass rates, aiming to shrink the town's subsidy of the beach program.
The Commission also voted, 3-0, to raise 2026 swim lesson rates, with a per-family cap for both residents and non-residents.
Staff said the new rates are still projected to fall short of covering the beach's costs, with the Parks revolving account as a possible backstop for the gap.
The Commission adopted an amended park facilities signage policy that removes the Commission itself from sign-approval authority, shifting it to staff.
Field-use rules and a proposed vendor-fair partnership were held off until a recreation director is hired, a position still vacant.

why_it_matters: This sets what residents and non-residents pay for beach passes and swim lessons in 2026, and it comes up in the context of a possible town override vote on covering town costs.
The rate increase is presented as narrowing, not closing, the gap between beach revenue and beach costs, so the shortfall may still draw on other town funds.
Sign approval at town park facilities now rests with staff rather than the elected Commission, changing who signs off on that kind of decision going forward.

ours.headline: Parks Commission voted to raise Town Beach and swim-lesson fees for 2026 to cut the town's subsidy.

watch_next: The independent peer review of the skate park cost estimate, once completed
A revised bonding/escrow proposal from the chair, town manager and town counsel, to be brought back to a public commission meeting

what_happened.line: The commission voted 4-0 to have the facilities director commission an independent peer review of the skate park's cost estimate, capped at an amount stated in the motion.
The vote followed doubts, including from the town manager, about whether the skate park consultant's estimate was high enough to size the town's bond correctly.
The skate park's representatives then proposed a donor-backed cash escrow in place of a traditional performance bond.

Rather than negotiate bond and escrow terms further in public, the chair, town manager and town counsel will work out a revised proposal with the skate park's representatives offline before returning to the commission.
No member proposed changing the lease agreement's existing rule that a lower restoration bond applies before the project is 50% complete and a higher completion bond applies after.

why_it_matters: The skate park is privately funded, but the town still needs a bond or equivalent security under the lease agreement to protect it if the project stalls or the builder cannot finish, which is what this review and the escrow proposal are meant to size correctly.
Members cited past projects, including the turf field and Marshall Park, as reasons to size security carefully rather than take the private estimate at face value.
The peer review's cost is expected to come from a revolving account, not general tax dollars, and the lease terms being renegotiated will determine what happens if the project is not completed.

ours.headline: Parks Commission voted to pay for an independent peer review of the skate park's roughly $1.14M cost estimate.

watch_next: Next regular meeting, February 25 — beach fee proposal expected back with figures and public feedback opportunity
Special meeting February 3, via Zoom, open to the public

what_happened.line: The Parks Commission opened discussion on roughly doubling town beach pass and lesson fees to make the beach self-sustaining, but took no vote.
The commission approved funding a replacement sign for Fitzgerald Field, to be paid from the parks revolving account.
The commission approved a private-donation project letting Lunenburg Youth Baseball demolish and rebuild two dugouts at Powell Field.
Draft field-use, signage, and non-resident field-fee policies were held for member redlines rather than adopted, to return next meeting.
The chair said town beach pass and lesson revenue covers about half of the beach's salary costs, with the town covering the rest.

why_it_matters: A resident beach-pass household could see rates move toward roughly double what they pay now, once a formal proposal comes back with numbers and public comment.
The push ties to town budget pressure: the commission is weighing whether beach and field fees should cover more of their own costs rather than draw on the town.
Non-resident and private-club field fees are also under review, which could change what outside youth sports organizations pay to use Lunenburg's fields.

ours.headline: Parks Commission floated roughly doubling town beach fees to keep it self-sustaining amid town budget cuts

watch_next: Next meeting: January 28th
Formal vote expected in January on the chair handling field-use paperwork while the recreation director position remains vacant

what_happened.line: The Parks Commission set aside the large Marshall Park project until the town's overall financial picture is clearer, with no work moving forward before January.
The commission will replace the storm-damaged Fitzgerald Field sign using parks funds once a cost is confirmed as reasonable.
A newer member took over the long-stalled beach house dedication sign project, honoring Genevieve Nass.
The commission kept youth sports per-player field fees unchanged for the spring season.
With the recreation director post still vacant, the chair plans to seek a formal vote in January to personally handle field-use paperwork in the meantime.

why_it_matters: Marshall Park's future, and any request for town-meeting funding, is on hold until the board revisits it in January -- residents should not expect a spring vote on the project.
The vacant, part-time recreation director position is affecting basic field-use administration, which could delay scheduling or policy fixes for youth leagues.
Youth sports families and leagues will pay the same per-player field fee this season, with written field-use policies still being drafted.

ours.headline: Parks Commission tables the roughly $14 million Marshall Park project until town finances are clearer.

watch_next: Anthony's report back on the restorative-bond figure from Chris Ruth
The Zoom meeting to vote on and execute the skate park contract

what_happened.line: The Parks Commission took no vote on the skate park bond, holding off until Anthony confirms a restorative-bond figure with town staff.
The board plans a short Zoom meeting to vote on and sign the skate park contract once that figure comes back, rather than waiting for its next regular meeting.
Repeated vandalism at Wallace Park's playground led to discussion of a noise-based deterrent device and hand-made signage, with no cost approved.
A member raised unresolved concern that the master plan's planned park location may shift once skate park construction begins at Marshall Park.

why_it_matters: The bond type the town requires for the skate park sets how much financial exposure the town carries if the project is not finished.
The contract vote is expected to happen at a short Zoom session rather than a regular posted meeting, which changes how residents can follow or weigh in.
Wallace Park's vandalism and the proposed deterrent touch a playground families currently use.

ours.headline: Parks Commission held off deciding the skate park bond amount, deferring to Chris Ruth's review first

watch_next: Town accountant's confirmation on the Marshall Park budget line, and revised cost estimates from the project's contractors
Next scheduled Parks Commission meeting, October 22

what_happened.line: The commission voted a fine against a resident for repeated unleashed-dog violations at McNiff Park despite a claimed ADA exemption.
The commission voted to make Fitzgerald Field regrading the top capital-plan priority, ahead of Northfield Park and other projects.
A discrepancy was found in the Marshall Park project's remaining budget and referred to the town accountant and manager.
The commission approved a community club's request to use the town beach for its annual fundraiser.

why_it_matters: The dog-fine vote tests how the town enforces park rules against a claimed ADA exemption, using a schedule that escalates on repeat offenses, while no dedicated park enforcement officer has yet been assigned.
The capital-plan ranking decides which park project the town funds first, directly affecting the ball field youth leagues use for games.
The Marshall Park budget discrepancy touches a federal ARPA grant with a year-end spending deadline, so how it is resolved could affect whether that funding is used or lost.

ours.headline: Parks Commission voted a $50 fine against a resident for repeated unleashed dogs at McNiff Park despite an ADA claim

watch_next: Revised skate park agreement terms at the commission's next meeting
Chris Ruth's capital planning item list, to be reviewed and prioritized before the next capital planning cycle

what_happened.line: The Parks Commission will not bring the Marshall Park project back to a town meeting vote this November, pushing it roughly a year out amid town-wide financial uncertainty.
The commission will keep spending remaining ARPA and capital funds to finish the Marshall Park design and engineering work.
The commission pulled its prior motion granting terms to the skate park group so the agreement can be revised at the next meeting.
Members left park user fees unchanged, deferring any change until reservation forms are redesigned to track actual field usage.
The commission dropped master-plan work for McNall and Northfield parks in favor of prioritizing Fitzgerald Field resurfacing on its capital list.

why_it_matters: Residents who expected a vote on Marshall Park at fall town meeting will not see one this cycle; the next opportunity is roughly a year out.

Park user fees, which members said cover only a fraction of maintenance and field costs, stay as they are for now, so any future increase will follow a usage review rather than happen at this meeting.
The skate park agreement returning to the table means its funding and construction terms are not yet final.

ours.headline: Commission will keep funding Marshall Park design but delay the next town-meeting vote about a year

page.overview:
It is the mission of the Personnel Committee to promote and maintain consistent and equitable standards in the administration of the Town's Personnel Bylaw, called the Salary Administration Plan, in conjunction with the Town Manager, and to represent the interests of both taxpayers and town employees.
Please use the navigation menu to locate past minutes and agendas. The next meeting agenda is posted there at least 48 hours prior to the meeting and often a week or more in advance.
The Personnel Committee is a five-member Committee appointed by the Select Board with each member serving for a term of three years. A Town employee may have a staff assignment to serve as a subject matter expert and non-voting member of the Personnel Committee.

page.overview:
If you choose to use the drop box located at the Lancaster Avenue entrance of the Ritter Building, please notify the Planning Board office.
The Planning Board consists of five members elected for terms of five years each. The Planning Board shall make careful studies of the resources, possibilities, and needs of the town and shall make plans for the development of the town. The Board shall make a comprehensive or master plan, setting forth in graphic and textual form policies to govern the future growth and development of the entire town. The Board shall have the power to regulate the subdivision of land within the town by the adoption of rules and regulations governing such development and the administration of such rules and regulations. The Planning Board shall make recommendations to the town meeting on all matters affecting land use and development, including the zoning by-laws of the town.
Zoning Bylaws are for sale at $35 per copy and the Rules and Regulations Governing the Subdivision of Land are for sale at $90 per copy. Both can be accessed on this page and are also available for purchase at the Planning Office, Ritter Memorial Building, 960 Massachusetts Avenue.

page.overview:
The Sewer Commission office is in the DPW Building at 520 Chase Road - the office is open from 7 am to 3 pm. The Commission regularly meets twice a month. The Commission meetings historically were held on the 2nd Tuesday (at the DPW Building) and the last Tuesday (in person at Town Hall) but check each posted agenda to be sure.
The Commission has been holding its meetings via Zoom. The links to the Zoom meetings are found with the posted agendas for public participation. Then the meeting recordings are found on the Lunenburg Access channel/YouTube.
The Sewer Commission is a five-member elected board. The Sewer Commission works in concert with the DPW and DPW Director to plan and implement changes, upgrades, and maintenance. Note: the Town's public water supply is administered by the Lunenburg Water District 978-582-4532 and is a separate entity from the Town. If you need a Betterment Payoff amount or Release of Lien, please Email Tax Collectors' Office or call 978-582-4132.
The Charter
The Sewer Commissioners shall make careful studies of the resources, possibilities, and needs of the Town as they relate to the availability of sanitary sewers and shall make plans for the installation of a system of sanitary sewers and for the maintenance of a sanitary sewer system. The Sewer Commission shall develop a comprehensive or master plan for a town-wide system of sanitary sewers, setting forth, in graphic and textual form, policies to govern the future growth and development of the entire Town. The Board of Sewer Commissioners shall, in conjunction with other land use bodies, assist in developing a long-range strategic plan for guiding town growth and development. The powers and authority of the Sewer Commission shall include oversight of the Sewer Enterprise Fund, setting rates and charges for the use of the sanitary sewer system, ratification responsibility for the Sewer Business Manager, and providing advice to the Board of Selectmen relating to intergovernmental agreements concerning sanitary sewers. The day-to-day operation, care, and maintenance of the sanitary sewers shall be under the supervision of the Town Manager. The Sewer Commission shall make an annual report to the Town Meeting, including a full accounting of the Sewer Enterprise Fund, information regarding the condition of the Town's sewer system and any plans or proposals for its development, and estimates of their cost.

page.overview:
Welcome to the Lunenburg Stormwater Task Force. The Stormwater Task Force is charged with the development of a comprehensive stormwater management plan that complies with state and federal regulations, provides a storm and surface water system that controls damage from storms, protects surface water quality and the environment. The plan shall determine which local agency or agencies will be responsible for implementation, establish the estimated cost of the program, as well as provide for the creation of an ongoing funding source to enable its success.
The Stormwater Task Force held its initial meeting on January 27, 2016.
We will provide information for citizens as we search through the plethora of data out there to determine what will be most useful. Please do not hesitate to email suggestions for inclusion.
All members are appointed by the Select Board. The group includes one member from the Select Board, Conservation Commission, and Planning Board. The Select Board voted to add two citizens-at-large (who live on local lakes) to the Stormwater Task Force in November 2021.
Learn more about the Stormwater Task Force (PDF)
Overview of Stormwater and the Stormwater Task Force- YouTube

page.overview:
From Town Charter, Section 4-1:
"The Town Manager shall be appointed by the Select Board from names submitted to it by a Town Manager Screening Committee which shall consist of 1 member of the Select Board, designated by it, 1 member of the School Committee, designated by it, 1 member of the planning board, designated by it, 1 member of the Finance Committee designated by it and the Town Moderator, who shall serve as the chair and call all meetings of the Town Manager Screening Committee. Whenever the position of Town Manager shall be vacant, the Town Manager Screening Committee shall be convened and shall solicit candidates, review applications, interview and rate candidates and submit the names of qualified candidates to the Select Board who shall appoint a Town Manager only from the names so prepared and submitted to it.
The Town Manager shall be a person especially fitted by education, training and previous experience in public administration and finance to perform the duties of the office. The Select Board shall appoint the Town Manager to serve for an indefinite term and shall fix the compensation for such person, annually, within the amount appropriated by the town. The Town Manager shall be appointed solely on the basis of demonstrated executive and administrative qualifications with special emphasis on financial matters. The Select Board may enter into a contract of employment with the town manager over wages, hours, benefits and other conditions of employment but no such contract shall be deemed to prevent the removal of the Town Manager by a majority vote of the full select board. The Town Manager need not be a resident of the town or of the commonwealth. The Town Manager shall not have served in an elective or appointive office in the town government for at least 365 days prior to appointment. The town may, from time to time, establish by by-law, such additional qualifications as seem necessary and appropriate."

The Board of Commissioners of Trust Funds shall have the management of all trust funds given or bequeathed for the benefit of the Town or the residents, unless the donor, in making the gift or bequest, shall make some other provision for the management of the fund. The Board shall, consistent with the terms of the trusts, manage and control said trusts, and distribute the income in accordance with the trusts.
There shall be a Board of Commissioners of Trust Funds consisting of 3 members who shall be elected for terms of 3 years each, so arranged that the term of 1 member shall expire each year.

page.overview:
Composition: The Lunenburg Board of Appeals consists of 5 members and 3 associate members, members are appointed by the Select Board for terms of five years and associate members for terms of three years.
Powers and Duties: The Zoning Board of Appeals shall hear and decide appeals, hear and decide applications for special permits upon which the Board is empowered to act, hear and decide petitions for variances. The Zoning Board of Appeals shall adopt rules, not inconsistent with the provisions of the Town Zoning Bylaws, for the conduct of its own business and shall file a copy of said rules with the Town Clerk. In exercising the powers granted to the Zoning Board of Appeals, the Board may make orders or decisions, reverse or affirm in whole or part, or modify any order or decision, and may issue or direct the issuance of a permit.
